newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH PRESIDENT RELAXES ANTI-ABORTION LAWS.
newsitem.headline: POLISH PRESIDENT RELAXES ANTI-ABORTION LAWS.

text.p: Taking side with the pro-choice liberals in defiance of the Vatican, President Aleksander Kwasniewski on Wednesday signed into law a bill relaxing Poland's strict anti-abortion rules.

Kwasniewski, a former communist turned into a social democrat, rejected calls from the Roman Catholic church and the right-wing oppostion to veto the bill, but called abortion an evil and urged work to eradicate its causes.
"Relaxation of the previous rules creates in Poland regulations similar to those adopted in other European countries," Kwasniewski said in a statement.
"I consider abortion evil. Its causes have to be liquidated and the state, the church and social organisations should cooperate in this respect," he added.

The law, pushed through parliament by co-ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance party (SLD), allows women to have abortion until the 12th week of pregnancy, after counselling, if she has personal or financial problems.
The regulations also provide for introducing sex education in schools and making cheap contraception easily available.

Under the previous law, passed in 1993 by a pro-church government, abortion was allowed only when a pregancy posed a threat to a woman's life, resulted from incest or rape, or the foetus was irreparably damaged.
Doctors, who broke the law, faced up to two years in prison. Several abortion trials have started over the last three years but none ended with a jail sentence.

Under the law, the number of officially registered abortions dropped to less than 1,000 from dozens of thousands in early 1990s but it also created a gynecological undeground. Better-off women were travelling abroad to terminate pregnancy.
The church, which had staged a vocal campaign against the relaxation of the abortion rules, strongly condemned the president's go-ahead for the law.
"Something really bad has happened. From the very begining we have described the bill as harmful to the Polish nation," bishop Tadeusz Pieronek told PAP news agency.
Kwasniewski said that a decision on abortion should be a matter of conscience and not result from the fear of punishment.

Former right-leaning president Lech Walesa, narrowly defeated by Kwasniewski 12 months ago, blocked a previous attempt by the ex-communists and other liberal left-wing parties to ease the abortion bill.

The outgoing law replaced communist-era regulations under which abortion was available virtually on demand. It was seen by more than half of the society as too strict, even though more than 90 percent of Poles describe themselves as Roman Catholics.
The new rules were condemned by the Polish-born Pope John Paul II, who is scheduled to visit his native land in mid-1997, several months before parliamentary elections.
The visit is widely expected to boost chances of the opposition parties rooted in the Solidarity movement, which overthrew communism in 1989 but lost power four years afterwards.
Some of these groups already pledge to again end the abortion freedom and analysts say the issue will be a major theme of the electoral campaign.
